target: AG1's claim that a national holiday would directly remove scheduling barriers and make voting easier for millions of eligible Americans.
objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to provide paid time off, so many low-income and hourly workers in retail, food service, care work, and similar sectors would still have to work and would still face the same time, wage, transport, and childcare constraints. The holiday therefore would not reliably eliminate the scheduling barrier for the people most affected.

target: AG1's assumption that a holiday would materially increase voting just by changing the calendar and making Election Day a celebration.
objection: A one-day election holiday does not address larger turnout obstacles such as registration problems, lack of early or absentee voting, long lines, polling-place accessibility, and procedural confusion. Reforms that directly expand voting access are more effective than a holiday alone.

target: AG2's claim that a federal holiday is merely a calendar shift and does not materially change who can vote.
objection: That objection underestimates the real-world effects of a holiday: it reduces family scheduling conflicts, especially childcare demands from school closures and school-day activities; it eases daily logistics like travel and errands when weekday routines disappear; and it can give hourly workers more feasible voting windows because many workplaces reduce operations or adjust hours on holidays.

target: AG1's broader claim that a federal holiday would reduce or eliminate work and school scheduling barriers.
objection: Because private employers are not required to provide paid holiday leave, many hourly workers in sectors that stay open on holidays would still need to work and would still lose wages if they took time to vote. So the holiday would not reliably solve the time-off problem for the most schedule-constrained voters.

target: AG2's argument that low-income workers would still face the same wage and staffing barriers on a holiday.
objection: Even without a legal mandate for paid leave, a national holiday changes the day’s broader schedule: schools and public services close or operate differently, childcare and transportation become easier to coordinate, and workplaces often adjust staffing and allow shift swapping. The barrier is not only paid leave, so a holiday can still meaningfully reduce scheduling constraints.

target: AG1's claim that a national holiday would lower voting barriers and improve access.
objection: A federal holiday can widen inequality because it mainly helps people who already have flexibility, while low-wage workers in open industries may still have to work and lose pay to vote. More targeted reforms—such as state laws requiring time off to vote and automatic voter registration—are more reliable and do not systematically disadvantage low-income workers.

target: AG2's contention that a holiday still leaves wage-constrained voters with the same time/money problem.
objection: The relevant barrier is broader than paid leave. A national holiday changes the whole coordination environment: schools and public services are closed, household logistics are easier, and shift patterns can become more flexible, creating actual windows for people to vote without needing legally guaranteed paid time off.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday would translate into higher turnout by reducing scheduling friction.
objection: Research and prior experience suggest that an election-day holiday by itself is not an effective turnout strategy compared with reforms that directly expand ballot access, such as required employer time off, early and absentee voting, streamlined registration, and more accessible polling options. The holiday may not reliably increase participation because other barriers remain in place.

target: AG1's assumption that school closures and a non-routine day make childcare and household logistics easier for voters.
objection: For many low-income families, school closures can make childcare less available and more expensive, not more accessible. If parents cannot take time off work, the holiday may simply shift the childcare problem rather than solve it, leaving them without a workable time to vote.

target: AG2's claim that school closures make childcare unavailable and that this means a holiday doesn't help families.
objection: That overstates the effect of school closures. A holiday can improve household coordination by aligning voting with a day when children are already out of school and workplace schedules are more flexible, so families may be able to rely on caregiver presence or shifted household coverage rather than expensive third-party childcare.
